newsitem.title: UK: Strong stg threatens UK manufacturing - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Strong stg threatens UK manufacturing - analysts.

text.p: The strength of sterling will become an increasing threat to the UK manufacturing sector despite further rises in official output data, analysts say.

"We are likely to see the strong exchange rate have a more significant effect on the official output data in coming months - so for manufacturers the worst may be yet to come," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC-Markets.
UK manufacturing output rose by just 0.3 percent in the three months to January, official data published on Wednesday showed.
UBS UK economist Andrew Cates said that activity was anaemic in manufacturing and said that survey evidence suggest the firm pound was damaging export orders.
"We would not expect the small recovery we have seen in the manufacturing sector to gather much momentum in the months ahead," he said.

He added that the data added to the weight of recent evidence that activity in the domestic economy might be slowing and there was therefore little necessity for a rise in Britain's 6.0 percent interest rates at the moment.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has been fending off requests from the Bank of England for a 1/4 point rise in interest rates.
But Morgan Stanley UK economist Kevin Gardiner argues that the output picture remains promising and says that healthy domestic demand will offset the negative impact on output of the dearer exports.
"Even for manufacturers, the biggest market is the domestic one," he said. "If consumers spend, manufacturing will grow. The pound is muting the rate of growth rather than stopping it altogether."

While Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist James Barty takes a similar view. "Sterling's strength is having an effect but manufacturing output continues to grow at a steady, if unspectacular rate, propped up by consumer demand."
However CIBC chief economist David Coleman says the January industrial production data hint at a slowdown in consumer related industries.
"We seem to be seeing a divergence in output related to consumers and output related to manufacturing industry. The strength all comes from areas like heavy engineering," he said.
By contrast, in the consumer related area of textiles, leather and clothing output fell by 1.4 percent in the latest quarter.

Analysts say that any slowdown in consumer activity is likely to be short-lived as consumer concentrate on paying off bills run-up in spending binges late in 1996. They are also holding on to their money because of uncertainty about the general elction, widely expected for May 1.

But once the election is out of the way, their spending is set to rise again reflecting windfall gains from flotations and mergers of building societies and tax cuts due to kick in in April, analysts say.
